title: WHEN “SUBMIT” BECOMES A WEAPON: The Difference Between Biblical Submission and Religious Bondage
paragraphs: WHEN “SUBMIT” BECOMES A WEAPON: The Difference Between Biblical Submission and Religious Bondage
Jesus never called you into a Christianity where another human being replaces your conscience, silences the truth, or demands the obedience that belongs to Christ alone.
There is a kind of bondage that does not look like bondage at first.
It carries a Bible.
It knows Christian vocabulary.
It says things like, “Respect authority.”
“Don’t touch the Lord’s anointed.”
“A godly wife submits.”
“Stop questioning and obey.”
“Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft.”
And sometimes, the person hearing those words is already so afraid of disappointing God that they surrender something God never commanded them to surrender.
Their discernment.
Their voice.
Their ability to say, “This is wrong.”
Their freedom to examine what they are being taught.
Sometimes even their safety.
That is what makes religious bondage so dangerous.
It can borrow the language of Scripture while violating the heart of Scripture.
And perhaps someone reading this has lived there.
You were not trying to rebel against God.
You were trying desperately to obey Him.
You stayed quiet because you thought silence was holiness.
You tolerated manipulation because you thought endurance was submission.
You stopped asking questions because somebody convinced you that questions were rebellion.
You allowed another human being to become so spiritually powerful in your life that disagreeing with them began to feel almost identical to disagreeing with God.
And somewhere inside you, something kept whispering:
This cannot be what Jesus meant.
That whisper deserves to be tested by Scripture.
Because biblical submission is real.
Authority is real.
Obedience is real.
Humility is real.
But so is religious bondage.
And confusing the two can leave sincere Christians defending chains that Jesus never placed around them.
One of the most important words in this conversation appears in Ephesians 5.
Paul writes:
The Greek reads:
ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ
Hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
The participle ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi) comes from ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō), carrying the idea of placing or arranging oneself under proper order or authority.
But notice what happens immediately before Paul discusses marriage.
ἀλλήλοις — allēlois.
“to one another.”
And notice the ultimate reference point:
ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ — en phobō Christou.
“In the fear/reverence of Christ.”
That changes the atmosphere of the entire discussion.
Christian submission does not begin with the unlimited power of one human being over another.
It begins under Christ.
Paul then speaks specifically to wives and husbands, but listen carefully to what husbands are commanded to do:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Christlike headship therefore cannot honestly be reduced to:
“You obey me.”
The model given to the husband is the crucified Christ.
Jesus gives Himself.
Jesus sacrifices.
Jesus loves.
Jesus washes feet.
Jesus protects His sheep.
Jesus does not use His authority to feed His ego.
And Jesus Himself exposed the pagan model of domination when His disciples were struggling with power.
“The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them… But ye shall not be so.” — Luke 22:25–26, KJV
Mark records the same revolutionary principle:
“Whosoever will be chief among you, shall be servant of all.” — Mark 10:44, KJV
Then Jesus points to Himself.
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
There is the Christian pattern of authority.
Not domination.
Service.
Not ego.
Sacrifice.
Not “How much control can I exercise?”
But “How much of myself am I willing to give for the good of those entrusted to me?”
That does not erase legitimate authority.
It defines what Christian authority is supposed to look like.
And that distinction matters enormously.

Because Scripture does command believers to submit to legitimate authority. Hebrews 13:17 speaks about obeying and submitting to spiritual leaders who watch over souls and will give account. Romans 13 discusses governing authorities. Children are commanded to obey their parents “in the Lord” in Ephesians 6:1. Wives are instructed concerning submission to their husbands in Ephesians 5:22–24 and Colossians 3:18.
We should not delete those passages because abusive people have misused them.
But neither should we delete the rest of the Bible to make those passages serve abusive people.
Scripture interprets Scripture.
And throughout Scripture, human authority remains human authority.
It never becomes God.
That boundary becomes unmistakable in Acts 5.
The apostles had been ordered not to teach in the name of Jesus.
Peter answered:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ Θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei Theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29, KJV
There is the line religious bondage desperately wants to blur.
God rather than men.
A Christian may submit to human authority.
A Christian may honor human authority.
A Christian may obey legitimate human authority.
But no Christian is permitted to transfer to another human being the ultimate allegiance that belongs to God.
Jesus Christ remains Lord.
That means biblical submission can never legitimately require you to participate in sin.
It cannot require you to call evil good.
It cannot require you to deny Christ.
It cannot require you to lie in order to protect someone's reputation.
It cannot require you to conceal criminal behavior.
It cannot require you to accept false teaching without examination.

It cannot require you to treat a pastor, husband, parent, ministry leader, prophet, apostle, teacher, denomination, or institution as though that person or organization were incapable of being questioned by Scripture.
Because the Bible itself praises people for examining teaching.
When Paul and Silas preached in Berea, Luke says the Bereans:
“received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.” — Acts 17:11, KJV
Think about that.
They examined apostolic preaching against Scripture.
And instead of condemning them for questioning authority, Scripture calls them noble.
Biblical authority does not need to fear biblical examination.
Truth does not panic when somebody opens the Bible.
Religious bondage does.
Bondage says:
“Don’t question me.”
Biblical leadership says:
“Test what I am saying by the Word of God.”
Bondage says:
“If you leave this church, you are leaving God.”
The Gospel says Christ has one universal body composed of His people, and no local leader owns the sheep Jesus purchased with His blood.
Bondage says:
“If you disagree with me, you are rebellious.”
Biblical humility remembers that even leaders remain accountable to Christ.
Bondage says:
“Protect the ministry's reputation.”
Biblical integrity says:
“Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.” — Ephesians 5:11, KJV
Bondage says:
“Your suffering proves your submission.”
But Scripture never turns needless participation in another person's sin into a Christian virtue.
This is where things become painfully personal.
Because some people did not remain in unhealthy situations because they were weak.
They remained because somebody attached the name of God to their captivity.
That is a particularly cruel form of manipulation.
When ordinary control says, “Do what I say,” you may recognize it.
But religious control says:
“God wants you to do what I say.”
Now the stakes feel eternal.
Suddenly saying no to a human being feels like saying no to Jesus.
Leaving feels like apostasy.
Setting a boundary feels like rebellion.
Reporting wrongdoing feels like betrayal.
And exposing darkness feels like attacking the church.
So you stay.
You shrink.
You apologize for things you did not do.
You learn to measure every sentence before speaking.
You become terrified of displeasing the person who claims to represent God.
Eventually you may no longer know where their voice ends and God's voice begins.
That is not spiritual maturity.
That is precisely why Christians need Scripture, the Holy Spirit, wisdom, accountable Christian community, and Jesus at the absolute center.
Paul wrote something remarkably strong to the Corinthians:
“Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy.” — 2 Corinthians 1:24, KJV
Read that again.
Paul was an apostle.
Yet he could say:
We do not dominate your faith.
That should make every Christian leader tremble before using spiritual authority to control another person's conscience.
Peter speaks similarly to elders.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.” — 1 Peter 5:3, KJV
The Greek contains the verb κατακυριεύω (katakurieuō), conveying the idea of exercising mastery or lordship over others.
Peter forbids elders from shepherding that way.
Why?
Because the sheep do not ultimately belong to the shepherd.
A few verses later Peter refers to:
“the chief Shepherd.” — 1 Peter 5:4, KJV
There is only one Chief Shepherd.
Jesus Christ.
Every pastor is under Him.
Every elder is under Him.
Every teacher is under Him.
Every husband is under Him.
Every parent is under Him.
Every government is under Him.
Every ministry is under Him.
Every Christian is under Him.
And therefore Christian submission is never permission for a human being to climb onto the throne that belongs to Jesus.
This does not mean that every correction is abuse.
That needs to be said clearly too.
Sometimes we call something “control” because we simply do not like being corrected.
Sometimes spiritual authority confronts genuine sin.
Sometimes parents must tell children no.
Sometimes church discipline is biblical.
Sometimes a spouse lovingly challenges destructive behavior.
Sometimes accountability hurts.
Sometimes the Bible itself cuts deeply.
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword…” — Hebrews 4:12, KJV
So the test cannot merely be:
“Did this make me uncomfortable?”
Jesus makes us uncomfortable sometimes.
Truth makes us uncomfortable.
Repentance certainly does.
The better questions are deeper.
Does this authority point me toward obedience to Christ, or toward dependence upon itself?
Can its claims be examined against Scripture?
Does it demand participation in sin?
Does it punish truthful questions merely because they threaten control?
Does leadership model sacrificial service or cultivate fear and personal loyalty?
Can wrongdoing be confronted?
Are leaders accountable?
Is Scripture being interpreted faithfully in context, or selectively weaponized?
Is my conscience being discipled under God's Word, or systematically replaced by somebody else's preferences?
And perhaps most revealing:
Who becomes bigger in my spiritual imagination?
Jesus?
Or the leader?
Because healthy Christian leadership should make Christ increasingly glorious.
Religious bondage makes the controller increasingly indispensable.
John the Baptist understood the difference.
Speaking of Christ, he said:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30, KJV
Every Christian ministry should carry something of that heartbeat.
Jesus bigger.
Us smaller.
Jesus remembered.
Us expendable.
Jesus followed.
Us merely pointing.
And this is where the Gospel enters the wound.
Because Jesus is not another manipulator competing for control over frightened people.
He is the Shepherd who laid His life down for His sheep.
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” — John 10:11, KJV
Religious bondage consumes sheep to preserve leaders.
Jesus gives Himself to save sheep.
Religious bondage hides scandal to protect institutions.
Jesus brings sinners into the light to redeem them.
Religious bondage says, “Perform well enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel says Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Religious bondage builds identity around fear.
The Gospel announces grace.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
The Christ who receives sinners calls sinners to repentance.
The Savior who breaks chains becomes our Lord.
Biblical freedom is therefore not independence from God.
It is liberation for God.
We are freed from the tyranny of sin so that we may belong joyfully to Christ.
This is the beautiful paradox Christianity refuses to surrender:
Freedom is found in belonging to Jesus.
Not because Christ is an abusive master.
But because the One to whom we belong is the One who was crucified for us.
The hands that hold authority over the Christian are scarred hands.
The King wore thorns.
The Shepherd became the Lamb.
The Judge took the judgment of His people upon Himself.
The Holy One welcomed scandalous sinners, then transformed them by grace.
That is why our story will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the woman who believed submission meant disappearing.
He rewrites the story of the man who confused spiritual leadership with domination.
He rewrites the story of the believer who spent years terrified of questioning a leader.
He rewrites the story of the leader who realizes, with horror, that he has used Scripture to control people and falls before Christ in repentance.
He rewrites the story of the church that chooses truth over reputation.
He rewrites the story of sinners like us.
Maybe your response to this article should not begin with someone else's sin.
Maybe it begins with your own heart.
Have I manipulated somebody in God's name?
Have I demanded obedience Scripture never gave me the right to demand?
Have I used “submission” because serving sacrificially was harder?
Have I remained silent about wrongdoing because exposing it might cost me relationships?
Have I confused pleasing people with pleasing God?
Have I resisted legitimate biblical correction and called it bondage simply because repentance hurt?
Every one of us needs the same place.
The cross.
No hiding.
No pretending.
No spiritual performance.
Just sinners standing before a Savior who already knows the truth.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your story. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending.
And please understand something else.
Send it privately to the believer who is afraid.

Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. Sometimes one faithful share places the Gospel in front of someone who would never have searched for it themselves.

Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor—grace cannot be bought, and nobody should give under spiritual compulsion. As Paul wrote, giving should be “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your freedom was purchased at a price.
Not so another human being could own your conscience.
Not so you could become your own god.
But so that, redeemed by grace, you could belong wholly to Jesus Christ.
Honor godly authority.
Receive biblical correction.
Practice humility.
Submit where Scripture commands submission.
Repent when you are wrong.
Forgive as Christ commands.
Serve.
Love.
But never hand a human being the throne that belongs to Jesus.
And if you have been using that throne yourself…
Get down.
There is grace at the foot of it.
There is forgiveness for repentant controllers and healing for wounded followers.
There is restoration for broken churches.
There is mercy for frightened believers.
There is hope for sinners.
Because Christianity's final word is not the scandal of what human beings did with power.
It is what Jesus did with His.
He laid it down in love, stretched out His hands on a cross, and turned the place of our condemnation into the doorway of our redemption.
The voice that demanded you surrender your conscience was never entitled to Christ's throne—and the Savior who truly sits there still bears scars from giving Himself for you.
